deep.reconstruction:
The page has two unrelated parts.

(A) Continuation of a programme on Dirichlet's theorem, begun on the previous page.

The opening parenthesis closes the previous page's sentence: '...as Tschebyscheff and Mertens have done (cf. the use of the Stirling series for complex arguments, after Stieltjes) for sum_{p<N} 1/q (q = every prime).'

Point 1, previous page. Hilbert asks whether the hard step of Dirichlet's proof can be bypassed. That step is showing L(1,chi) != 0. Here L_{+1} and L_{-1} denote the L-series at s=1 for the real non-principal character(s), for example the quadratic character of a prime modulus.
- The proposed alternative starts from the cyclotomic polynomial. A prime dividing Phi_k(n) and not dividing k satisfies q ≡ 1 (mod k), i.e. q = kp+1 in Hilbert's notation.
- He would then estimate the sum sum_{p<N} 1/q directly over such primes q.
- The model is Mertens' 1874 elementary theorem, sum_{p<=N} 1/p = log log N + M + o(1), and Chebyshev's estimates.
- In modern terms he wants a Mertens-type asymptotic for primes ≡ 1 (mod k), namely sum_{q<=N, q≡1(k)} 1/q = (1/phi(k)) log log N + O(1), obtained without L-functions.
- No computation is carried out.

Point 2. Dirichlet's proof that L_{+1}, L_{-1} != 0 'can in any case be simplified' by applying formula §58, p.157 of G.F. Meyer, Vorlesungen über die Theorie der bestimmten Integrale. Dirichlet expressed the L-series through definite integrals of the form ∫_0^1 x^{s-1} f(x)/(1-x^k) dx.
- Hilbert then asks whether definite integrals can be avoided altogether, perhaps via Schlömilch, Compendium der höheren Analysis II (1866), p.242 (Gamma function).
- The Gamma-function route is the standard one: L(1,chi) = -(1/k) sum_a chi(a) psi(a/k), which also gives the Gauss-type closed forms.
- This is a reading note only; no derivation is given.

(B) The solvability claim.

Hilbert asserts that every mathematical problem reduces to the following form.
- Given: a law T ('Gesetz') that assigns to every infinite 0-1 sequence alpha (e.g. 001100...) another infinite 0-1 sequence beta = T(alpha) (e.g. 100111...).
- T must be built from 'sequence operations': taking the greatest integer, searching for divisors, and so on, but explicitly not dice-throwing ('nicht Würfeln'). So T is deterministic and effective.
- The task: decide by finitely many operations whether some output sequence beta contains a 0, or whether every beta consists only of 1s.
- In modern form: decide the truth of 'for all alpha in 2^N, for all n: T(alpha)(n) = 1'. For a fixed alpha this is a Pi^0_1 statement; quantifying over alpha makes it Pi^1_1-like.

Hilbert's thesis: every such decision is possible by finitely many sequence operations. There is no law for which it fails. He states three equivalent slogans:
- every mathematical problem is solvable;
- everything reachable by human understanding through pure thought, without matter, can also be resolved;
- 'there is only one problem'.
His examples are the quadrature of the circle and 'does pi = 3.14... contain 10 consecutive 7s?'. He closes: 'One assumes possibility from the outset.' This is the germ of the no-ignorabimus axiom of 1900, here in a quasi-formal, sequence-transformation framing of the decision problem.
errors: Nothing on the page is a derivation, so there are no computational errors.

The decidability thesis is false in modern light. Church and Turing (1936) showed there are effective T for which 'all outputs are all-1' is undecidable. Gödel's incompleteness theorems show some such questions are not even settled by a fixed formal system.

The proposed bypass of L(1,chi) != 0 via cyclotomic polynomials gives infinitely many primes ≡ 1 mod k, as in Sylvester/Lebesgue. It does not by itself give the density statement for that class. For other residue classes a ≢ 1 the cyclotomic trick does not work at all (Murty's criterion: only a^2 ≡ 1). The hope is therefore justified only for the class 1 mod k.

Treating 'quadrature of the circle' as an open problem is anachronistic. Lindemann had already settled it in 1882; Hilbert presumably means it as an example of a problem once thought hopeless that turned out solvable.

results.what: Reduction of every mathematical problem to deciding whether an effective 0-1 sequence transformation ever outputs a 0, with the thesis that every such question is decidable in finitely many steps
results.modern_name: Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem / no-ignorabimus thesis; Pi^0_1 (halting-type) normal form of mathematical statements
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert 1900 (Paris address, solvability axiom); Entscheidungsproblem formulated by Hilbert–Ackermann 1928; refuted by Church and Turing 1936

results.what: Digits of pi (10 consecutive 7s) used as the paradigm of an open decision question
results.usually_credited_to: L.E.J. Brouwer (from c.1908, the sequence 0123456789 in pi)

results.what: Plan to avoid L(1,chi) != 0 via cyclotomic polynomials plus a Mertens-type estimate for primes ≡ 1 mod k
results.modern_name: Elementary/Euclidean proofs of Dirichlet's theorem for 1 mod k; Mertens' theorem in arithmetic progressions
results.usually_credited_to: Sylvester, Lebesgue, Wendt (infinitude of primes ≡ 1 mod k); Mertens 1874; Selberg 1949 (elementary Dirichlet)

results.what: Simplifying the non-vanishing proof via Gamma-function formulas instead of definite integrals
results.usually_credited_to: Dirichlet, Gauss, Kummer; textbook material (Schlömilch, G.F. Meyer)

deep.surprise_reason: Hilbert's belief in the solvability of every problem is famous from 1900. This note is probably early: it cites a Stieltjes 1889 reference and appears among youthful study plans. What is notable is the quasi-formal setting: problems become questions about effective, non-random transformations of infinite binary sequences, and the decision asks whether some output contains a 0. That anticipates the Entscheidungsproblem and the Pi^0_1/halting normal form decades early. The pi-digit example also predates Brouwer's use of it. These notebooks are known to historians and the passage may already be quoted, so this is a notable unpublished detail, not a new theorem.

checkable.sympy: all(isprime(q) and ((q-1) % 7 == 0 or q == 7) for n in range(2,40) for q in factorint(cyclotomic_poly(7, n)).keys())
checkable.asserts: Prime divisors of Phi_7(n) are 7 or ≡ 1 mod 7, the 'Kreisteilungsgleichung' fact Hilbert invokes.

checkable.sympy: N(sum(1/Integer(p) for p in primerange(2, 10**6)) - log(log(10**6)))
checkable.asserts: This is approximately Mertens' constant 0.2615, illustrating Mertens' theorem sum 1/p = log log N + M + o(1).
L(1,chi_{-4}) = pi/4, which is nonzero: an instance of L_{-1} != 0.
Gamma/digamma formula L(1,chi) = -(1/k) sum chi(a) psi(a/k) for k=4: the Gamma-function route to L(1,chi) without definite integrals (result 0).

transcription_corrections: Line 3: 'Der Dirichletsche Beweis für ≠ +1, ≠ -1, ≠ 0' should read 'für L_{+1}, L_{-1} ≠ 0'. The symbols are the L-series of the previous page.
'Meyer[?]: bestimmte Integrale' refers to G. F. Meyer, Vorlesungen über die Theorie der bestimmten Integrale; the reading 'Meyer' is plausible.

'[-Etwa-] indem man...' reads more like a cancelled 'Etwa' followed by 'indem man Schlömilch Compendium II 1866 pag 242 (Gammafunktion)'. The year is written as 18[6/7]6 with an overwrite and is most likely 1866.
'ob alle Reihen (β) nur Einsen bestehen' should be 'nur aus Einsen bestehen'.
The opening parenthesis '(Vgl. Benutzung der Stirlingschen Reihe für complexe Argumente nach Stieltjes)' is a bracketed insertion belonging to the previous page's sentence ending '...gethan haben'.
